periods.name: Through the Sea into the Wilderness

events.title: Slavery in Egypt
events.subtitle: A king who did not know Joseph, and sons thrown into the river
story: The rich land of Goshen in the Nile Delta. The seventy members of Jacob's family who had come down with him multiplied over the years until they filled the fields. But when a new king arose who did not know Joseph, the neighbours of yesterday became, overnight, a crowd to be watched and feared.

Under the burning sun the sound of mud being trodden and bricks being baked never stopped. The taskmasters' whips drove them to build the store cities of Pithom and Rameses. Yet the more they were oppressed, the more Israel flourished, and the fear of the Egyptians grew deeper with it.

Pharaoh ordered the Hebrew midwives Shiphrah and Puah to kill the baby boys, but they feared God and let the infants live. At last the king gave an order to all his people. Every Hebrew boy was to be thrown into the river. The waters of the Nile flowed dark.

words.text: Look, the people of Israel have grown more numerous and stronger than we are. If war breaks out they may join our enemies and fight against us. Let us deal with them shrewdly.
Hebrew women are not like Egyptian women. They are strong, and they give birth before the midwife even arrives.
Every boy born to the Hebrews, throw into the Nile. You may let the girls live.

events.note: Pithom and Rameses were store cities where grain and supplies were kept. Because of the name Rameses, some date the exodus to the thirteenth century BC under Ramesses II, but this journey follows the earlier date given in 1 Kings 6:1.
events.reflect: If Scripture keeps the names of two midwives instead of the king's, whose eyes do I fear when I make my choices where no one is watching?

quiz.q: What were the names of the midwives who defied Pharaoh and saved the Hebrew babies?
quiz.explain: The midwives Shiphrah and Puah feared God; they did not do as the king commanded but let the boys live (Ex 1:15–17). God gave them families of their own (Ex 1:21).

img.credit: James Tissot, Pharaoh Notes the Importance of the Jewish People, c. 1896–1902 · The Jewish Museum, New York · Public domain

events.title: A Basket on the Nile
events.subtitle: A baby drawn out of the river
story: A woman of the house of Levi gave birth to a son. He was a fine-looking child, and his mother hid him for three months. As his cries grew louder, there were fewer places to hide him. At last she wove a small basket from papyrus stalks and coated it with tar and pitch.

On the bank of the Nile, where the morning light broke on the water, the mother laid the baby in the basket and set it among the reeds. While the reeds rustled in the wind, the baby's sister stood at a distance, holding her breath to see what would happen to it.

Pharaoh's daughter came down to bathe in the river and found the basket among the reeds. When she opened it, the baby was crying, and her heart was moved. Thanks to his sister's quick thinking, the child went back to his own mother's arms to be nursed. The princess adopted him as her son and named him Moses.

words.text: This must be one of the Hebrew babies.
Shall I go and find one of the Hebrew women to nurse the baby for you?
I drew him out of the water, so his name will be Moses.

events.note: The name Moses sounds like the Hebrew word masha, to draw out. Others think it comes from an Egyptian word meaning son or born of, as in the name Thutmose. The names of his parents, Amram and Jochebed, appear in Exodus 6:20.
events.reflect: If the very river that carried the order of death became the way a baby was rescued, do I believe God can work even in the place I fear most?

quiz.q: How long did Moses' mother hide him before putting him in the basket?
quiz.explain: Seeing that he was a fine child, his mother hid him for three months, and when she could hide him no longer she made the papyrus basket (Ex 2:2–3).

img.title: Moses Laid Amid the Flags
img.credit: James Tissot, Moses Laid Amid the Flags, c. 1896–1902 · The Jewish Museum, New York · Public domain

events.title: Flight to Midian
events.subtitle: A prince sheds his robes and becomes a stranger
story: Raised in the palace, Moses grew up and went out to where his own people were labouring. He saw an Egyptian beating a Hebrew. Looking this way and that, he struck the Egyptian down and hid him in the sand. He thought no one had seen.

The next day he tried to stop two Hebrews who were fighting, and the one in the wrong shot back, asking whether he meant to kill him too, as he had killed the Egyptian the day before. What Moses thought no one had seen was already known. The story reached Pharaoh, and the king sought to kill Moses. Moses left everything behind and fled across the eastern wilderness to the land of Midian.

At a well in Midian, Moses came to the aid of seven sisters whom the shepherds were driving away, and he watered their flock. He stayed in the house of their father Reuel, married Zipporah, and had a son, Gershom. Meanwhile in Egypt the groaning of Israel rose up to heaven, and God heard it.

words.text: Who made you our ruler and judge? Are you planning to kill me the way you killed that Egyptian yesterday?
Where is he now? Why did you leave the man behind? Go and invite him to eat with us.
I have become a stranger in a foreign land.

events.note: Midian is thought to have been the land of nomadic peoples east of the Gulf of Aqaba, in the northwest of the Arabian Peninsula. In chapter 3 Reuel is called Jethro. Stephen says Moses was forty years old when he went to visit his own people.
events.reflect: If it was not forty years in the palace but forty years in the wilderness that shaped Moses, am I treating the hidden years after my failure as nothing but wasted time?

quiz.q: What was the name of the first son born to Moses in Midian?
quiz.explain: Moses named his son Gershom, saying, I have become a stranger in a foreign land (Ex 2:22). Eliezer is the second son, mentioned later in Exodus 18:4.

img.credit: James Tissot, Moses Slays an Egyptian, c. 1896–1902 · The Jewish Museum, New York · Public domain

events.title: The Burning Bush
events.subtitle: A fire that burned but did not consume
story: Tending the flock of his father-in-law Jethro, Moses went deep into the wilderness and came to Horeb, the mountain of God. On a quiet slope of nothing but rock and dry scrub, a single bush was wrapped in flames. Yet strangely, the bush was not burning up at all.

As he came closer, a voice called to him from within the fire. Moses, Moses. Told to take off his sandals, he stood barefoot on the hot ground and hid his face, afraid to look at God. The Lord said he had heard the cry of his people in slavery.

Who am I to go to Pharaoh? Moses held back again and again. The Lord told him his name and showed him signs: a staff that became a snake, a hand that turned white. To the man who said he was no speaker, he gave his brother Aaron, and he said, I will be with you.

words.text: I am who I am. Tell the people of Israel this: I Am has sent me to you.
I have clearly seen the suffering of my people in Egypt, and I have heard them cry out. I know their pain. Now I have come down to rescue them.
Who gave people their mouths? Is it not I, the Lord? Now go. When you speak, I will be with your mouth.
Who am I, that I should go to Pharaoh and bring the people of Israel out of Egypt?

events.note: Horeb is taken to be another name for Mount Sinai. Tradition places it at Jebel Musa in the southern Sinai Peninsula, where Saint Catherine's Monastery stands at its foot, but other views place it in the northern Sinai or in the land of Midian in northwestern Arabia.
events.reflect: When Moses asked who he was to go, God answered not with his qualifications but with the promise “I will be with you”; am I still searching for that answer inside myself?

quiz.q: Before the burning bush, what did God first tell Moses to take off?
quiz.explain: God said, Do not come any closer. Take off your sandals, for the place where you are standing is holy ground (Ex 3:5).

img.title: Landscape with Moses and the Burning Bush
img.credit: Domenichino, Landscape with Moses and the Burning Bush, c. 1610–1616 · The Metropolitan Museum of Art · Public domain

events.title: Before Pharaoh
events.subtitle: Make bricks without straw
story: Moses and Aaron stood in Pharaoh's palace. When they said that the God of Israel was telling him to let his people go to hold a festival in the wilderness, the king laughed coldly. Who is the Lord, that I should listen to him? That day the king's command came back as an even heavier burden.

From now on you will get no straw to mix into the bricks; go and gather it yourselves. But do not make a single brick fewer. The people scattered across all Egypt hunting for stubble instead of straw, and the Israelite foremen were beaten when the quota was not met.

Soon the blame was poured out on Moses. Heartbroken, he took his complaint to God. Why have you brought trouble on this people? The Lord promised again that he would rescue them and make them his own people. But worn down by their cruel labour, the people no longer had the strength even to listen.

words.text: I am the Lord. I will bring you out from under the heavy burdens of Egypt and rescue you with an outstretched arm. I will take you as my people, and I will be your God.
Now you will see what I do to Pharaoh. Pressed by a mighty hand, he will let the people go.
Who is the Lord, that I should obey him and let Israel go? I do not know the Lord, and I will not let Israel go.

events.note: Egyptian bricks were made by mixing straw into Nile mud and drying it in the sun. The straw held the bricks together so they would not crack. A wall painting in the tomb of Rekhmire at Thebes shows foreign labourers shaping bricks.
events.reflect: When obedience brought back only a heavier burden, Moses demanded to know why; can I accept even such an honest prayer as part of faith?

quiz.q: What did Pharaoh say he would no longer give the Israelites?
quiz.explain: Pharaoh said, Do not give them straw for the bricks as before; let them gather it themselves, and he did not let them reduce the number of bricks (Ex 5:7–8).

img.credit: James Tissot, Moses Speaks to Pharaoh, c. 1896–1902 · The Jewish Museum, New York · Public domain

events.title: The Ten Plagues
events.subtitle: Ten signs upon a hardened heart
story: When Moses raised his staff and struck the river, the Nile turned red, the fish died, and a stench spread. Then frogs crept up even into the palace bedrooms, and the dust became gnats swarming over people and animals. The magicians who had copied the signs finally gave up.

Swarms of flies came, but they passed over the land of Goshen. Livestock sickened and fell, boils broke out on people's bodies, and hail struck the fields with thunder. Locusts devoured every green thing that was left, and for three days a darkness so thick it could almost be touched covered the land.

Even in that darkness there was light where the people of Israel lived. Pharaoh would bow his head, then harden his heart again as soon as a plague stopped. At last Moses announced the final plague. At midnight every firstborn in Egypt would die. A heavy silence settled over the land.

words.text: Let my people go, so that they may worship me in the wilderness.
This time I will send all my plagues on you, your officials and your people, so that you will know there is no one like me in all the earth.
This is the finger of God.

events.note: The plagues are sometimes read as judgments on the gods Egypt worshipped, such as the Nile and the sun. The Lord himself said he would bring judgment on all the gods of Egypt. Some try to explain the plagues as a chain of natural events, but views differ.
events.reflect: Pharaoh's heart did not harden all at once but a little more each time a plague stopped; whenever I get room to breathe, what am I putting off as my heart hardens?

quiz.q: Which plague could the Egyptian magicians not copy, leading them to say it was the finger of God?
quiz.explain: When Aaron struck the dust of the ground with his staff, it became gnats. The magicians could not produce gnats and said, This is the finger of God (Ex 8:16–19).

img.credit: James Tissot, Water Is Changed into Blood, c. 1896–1902 · The Jewish Museum, New York · Public domain

events.title: The First Passover
events.subtitle: Blood on the doorposts, a night passed over
story: The Lord told them to make this month the first month of the year. Each household chose a year-old lamb without blemish and slaughtered it at dusk on the fourteenth day of that month. They dipped a bunch of hyssop in the blood and put it on the two doorposts and the lintel above. The red marks glistened in the evening light.

That night, with belts fastened, sandals on and staffs in hand, they hurriedly ate roasted meat, unleavened bread and bitter herbs. At midnight a wail went up across all Egypt. From the firstborn son of the palace to the firstborn of the prisoner in the dungeon, there was no house without its dead.

That same night Pharaoh summoned Moses and Aaron and urged them to leave. The people wrapped their unrisen dough, bowls and all, in their cloaks, slung it over their shoulders, and set out from Rameses. About six hundred thousand men left on foot. It was the night that ended four hundred and thirty years of slavery.

words.text: The blood will be a sign on the houses where you live. When I see the blood, I will pass over you. No plague will touch you when I strike Egypt.
Eat it in haste, with your belt fastened, your sandals on your feet and your staff in your hand. This is the Lord's Passover.
Get up and leave my people, you and the Israelites. Go and worship the Lord as you said. And ask a blessing for me too.

events.note: The Hebrew word for Passover, Pesach, is linked to the idea of passing over. Israel still remembers this night every year. The last meal Jesus shared with his disciples was also a meal at Passover time.
events.reflect: If what kept Israel safe that night was not their goodness but the blood on the doorposts, am I still looking for the grounds of my salvation in my own goodness?

quiz.q: According to Exodus 12, how long did the Israelites live in Egypt?
quiz.explain: At the end of four hundred and thirty years, on that very day, all the Lord's hosts went out of the land of Egypt (Ex 12:40–41).

img.credit: James Tissot, The Signs on the Door, c. 1896–1902 · The Jewish Museum, New York · Public domain

events.title: Pillar of Cloud and Fire
events.subtitle: Not the short road, but the wilderness
story: The crowd that left Rameses reached Succoth. The road along the coast through the land of the Philistines was the shortest, but God did not lead them that way. He was concerned that if they faced war, the people would change their minds and go back to Egypt.

Moses took the bones of Joseph with him. Centuries before, Joseph had made them swear to carry his bones up from Egypt. They camped at Etham on the edge of the wilderness. By day a pillar of cloud cast its shade, and by night a pillar of fire lit up the desert darkness.

Day and night the pillar never left its place in front of the people. Then the Lord had them turn back and camp before Pi Hahiroth, between Migdol and the sea. It looked like a shore with no way out. It was meant to make Pharaoh think they were trapped in the wilderness.

words.text: If these people see war, they may change their minds and go back to Egypt.
I will harden Pharaoh's heart, and he will pursue you. Through Pharaoh and his army I will show my glory, and the Egyptians will know that I am the Lord.
God will surely come to help you. When he does, carry my bones up from this place.

events.note: The Way of the Philistines was the great road along the Mediterranean coast to Canaan, guarded by Egyptian fortresses. Succoth is thought to be Tell el Maskhuta, but the sites of Etham, Migdol and Pi Hahiroth are still uncertain.
events.reflect: If God led them by the wilderness road rather than the short way because he knew how weak they were, can I receive my own long way round as care rather than punishment?

quiz.q: What did Moses take with him out of Egypt?
quiz.explain: Moses took the bones of Joseph with him, because Joseph had made the Israelites swear to carry his bones up from Egypt (Ex 13:19; Gen 50:25).

img.title: The Israelites Leaving Egypt
img.credit: David Roberts, The Israelites Leaving Egypt, 1829 · Birmingham Museum and Art Gallery · Public domain

events.title: The Sea Divides
events.subtitle: Dry ground in the middle of the sea
story: Regretting that he had let the people go, Pharaoh pursued them with six hundred of his best chariots and all the chariots of Egypt. As Israel, camped by the sea, looked up, the sound of hooves came closer through a cloud of dust. The sea lay ahead, and an army behind.

Were there no graves in Egypt, that you brought us out to die in the wilderness? Over the people's screams Moses cried out: do not be afraid, stand still and see the Lord's salvation. The pillar of cloud moved behind the camp and split the night, dark on one side and bright on the other.

Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and all night a strong east wind blew. The waters parted and the seabed dried. The people walked across between waters standing like walls on either side. Toward dawn the chariot wheels sank in the mud, and the returning waves covered the Egyptian army. The people feared the Lord and believed.

words.text: Why are you crying out to me? Tell the Israelites to move forward. Raise your staff, stretch out your hand over the sea and divide it.
Do not be afraid. Stand still and see the salvation the Lord will bring you today. The Lord will fight for you; you need only be still.
Let us get away from Israel. The Lord is fighting for them against us.

events.note: In Hebrew, Yam Suph means sea of reeds. Where the crossing took place is debated. Suggestions include the lakes of the Isthmus of Suez, such as Lake Ballah, Lake Timsah and the Bitter Lakes, as well as the Gulf of Suez and the Gulf of Aqaba.
events.reflect: If “Stand still and see” and “Move forward” belong to the same scene, which faith do I need today: the faith that stops and waits, or the faith that takes one step onto the wet seabed?

quiz.q: How did God drive the sea back all night?
quiz.explain: When Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, the Lord drove the sea back all night with a strong east wind and turned it into dry land (Ex 14:21).

img.title: The Waters Are Divided
img.credit: James Tissot, The Waters Are Divided, c. 1896–1902 · The Jewish Museum, New York · Public domain

events.title: The Song by the Sea
events.subtitle: The first praise, over the beat of tambourines
story: Morning broke over the shore. Broken pieces of chariots washed up on the calm waves, and the survivors stood on the wet sand. Then Moses and the Israelites lifted their voices and began to sing. It was a song to the Lord, who had hurled horse and rider into the sea.

The Lord is my strength and my song. The words remember the blast of breath that split the sea and the waters that stood up like a wall, and they look ahead. Philistia, Edom, Moab and Canaan will tremble, and the Lord will lead this people and plant them on his holy mountain.

Then Miriam the prophet, Aaron's sister, took a tambourine in her hand. All the women followed her with tambourines, dancing. Over the sound of the tambourines carried on the sea breeze, Miriam's voice rang out, leading the song. Sing to the Lord, for he has triumphed gloriously.

words.text: The Lord is my strength and my song; he is the one who saved me. He is my God, and I will praise him; my father's God, and I will lift him high.
Lord, who among the gods is like you? Who shines in holiness, awesome in praise, doing wonders?
Sing to the Lord, for he has won a great victory. Horse and rider he has thrown into the sea.

events.note: Because of its many archaic Hebrew expressions, this Song of the Sea is considered one of the oldest poems in the Bible. Miriam is the first woman in the Bible called a prophet, and the book of Revelation also pictures people singing the song of Moses.
events.reflect: As the song by the sea went beyond the enemy's fall to praise the Lord as my strength and my song, does my gratitude stop at what happened, or does it reach the one who did it?

quiz.q: What did the prophet Miriam hold in her hand as she sang with the women?
quiz.explain: Miriam the prophet, Aaron's sister, took a tambourine, and all the women followed her with tambourines and dancing (Ex 15:20).

img.title: The Songs of Joy
img.credit: James Tissot, The Songs of Joy, c. 1896–1902 · The Jewish Museum, New York · Public domain

events.title: Bitter Water Made Sweet
events.subtitle: The first thirst, where the singing stopped
story: As the song by the sea died away, Moses led the people into the Wilderness of Shur. They walked for three days and found no water. The sand underfoot grew burning hot, and one by one the waterskins ran empty.

At last they reached Marah and found water, but it was too bitter to drink. The people grumbled against Moses, asking what they were supposed to drink. Moses cried out to the Lord, and the Lord showed him a piece of wood. He threw it into the water, and the bitter water turned sweet.

There the Lord gave the people a decree and put them to the test. If they listened to his voice, he would not bring on them the diseases he had brought on Egypt. Then they came to Elim. In the shade of twelve springs and seventy palm trees, they pitched their tents by the water.

words.text: If you listen carefully to the voice of the Lord your God and do what is right in my eyes, I will not bring on you any of the diseases I brought on Egypt. I am the Lord who heals you.
What are we supposed to drink?

events.note: Marah means bitter in Hebrew. Some identify Marah with Ain Hawara on the eastern shore of the Gulf of Suez and Elim with Wadi Gharandel, but the exact locations of both are unknown and views differ.
events.reflect: If what made the bitter water sweet was not the water but the wood thrown into it, what am I throwing into the bitter places of my life: complaint, or a cry to God?

quiz.q: What was at Elim, the place they reached after Marah?
options: Twelve springs and seventy palm trees
Seven springs and twelve palm trees
One well and forty fig trees
Three springs and seventy olive trees
quiz.explain: At Elim there were twelve springs and seventy palm trees, and the people camped there by the water (Ex 15:27).

img.title: Moses Sweetening the Bitter Waters of Marah
img.credit: Nicolas Poussin, Moses Sweetening the Bitter Waters of Marah, c. 1629–1630 · Baltimore Museum of Art · Public domain

events.title: Manna from Heaven
events.subtitle: Each morning, a day's bread on the dew
story: A little over a month after leaving Egypt, on the fifteenth day of the second month, the people entered the Wilderness of Sin between Elim and Sinai. When hunger struck, they grumbled against Moses and Aaron, saying they wished they had died in Egypt, where they sat by pots of meat and ate their fill.

In the evening quail flew in and covered the camp. In the morning, when the dew lifted, something fine and white like frost lay over the wilderness. When the people asked what it was, Moses told them it was the bread the Lord had given them to eat. It tasted like wafers made with honey.

They were told to gather an omer for each person, just enough for the day. Whatever was kept until morning bred worms and began to smell. On the sixth day they gathered twice as much and kept the Sabbath. Israel ate this manna for forty years, until they came to the border of Canaan, a land where people lived.

words.text: Look, I will rain down bread from heaven for you. Each day the people are to go out and gather just enough for that day.
At twilight you will eat meat, and in the morning you will be filled with bread. Then you will know that I am the Lord your God.
This is the bread the Lord has given you to eat.

events.note: The name manna is explained as coming from the Hebrew man hu, meaning what is it. An omer was a tenth of an ephah, thought to be a little over two litres. Aaron put an omer of manna in a jar and placed it before the tablets of the covenant.
events.reflect: Manna could not be stored, so it made them look to heaven every day; are the things I store up for tomorrow robbing me of my reason to look to God today?

quiz.q: For how many years did the Israelites eat manna?
quiz.explain: The Israelites ate manna for forty years, until they came to a land where people lived, the border of Canaan (Ex 16:35).

img.title: The Gathering of the Manna
img.credit: James Tissot, The Gathering of the Manna, c. 1896–1902 · The Jewish Museum, New York · Public domain

events.title: Water from the Rock
events.subtitle: Is the Lord among us or not?
story: Leaving the Wilderness of Sin, they passed through several places and camped at Rephidim, but there was no water to drink there either. The sun beat down on the rocky valley, and the camp was filled with the cries of thirsty children and animals. The people quarrelled with Moses, demanding water.

Moses cried out to the Lord. What shall I do with this people? Soon they will stone me. The Lord told him to take some of the elders and the staff with which he had struck the Nile, and to walk on ahead of the people. I will stand before you there on the rock at Horeb, he said.

As the elders watched, Moses struck the rock, and water gushed out and flowed. Moses called the place Massah and Meribah, because the people had quarrelled and had tested the Lord, asking, Is the Lord among us or not?

words.text: Look, I will stand before you there on the rock at Horeb. Strike the rock, and water will burst out of it for the people to drink.
Why do you quarrel with me? Why do you put the Lord to the test?
What am I to do with these people? A little more and they will stone me.

events.note: Rephidim is thought to be near Wadi Feiran in the southern Sinai Peninsula, but this is uncertain. Massah means testing and Meribah means quarrelling, and Psalm 95 recalls this event as an example of a hardened heart.
events.reflect: Even on the day they quarrelled over whether the Lord was among them, God was already standing on that rock; in the middle of my thirst, do I believe he got there before me?

quiz.q: What names did Moses give the place where water came from the rock?
quiz.explain: Because the people quarrelled and tested the Lord, Moses called the place Massah and Meribah (Ex 17:7).

img.title: Moses Strikes the Rock
img.credit: James Tissot, Moses Strikes the Rock, c. 1896–1902 · The Jewish Museum, New York · Public domain

events.title: Two Raised Hands
events.subtitle: Hands that did not come down until sunset
story: Amalek attacked at Rephidim. Moses told Joshua to choose men and go out to fight, while he himself climbed to the top of the hill with the staff of God in his hand. Aaron and Hur stood beside him. The clash of swords rose from the valley below.

Whenever Moses held up his hands, Israel prevailed, and whenever he lowered them, Amalek prevailed. As time went on and his arms grew heavy, the two men brought a stone for him to sit on and held up his hands, one on each side. His hands stayed steady until the sun went down.
Joshua defeated Amalek with the sword. The Lord told Moses to write this down in a book as a reminder and to make sure Joshua heard it. Moses built an altar and called it The Lord Is My Banner.

words.text: Write this in a book as a reminder, and make sure Joshua hears it. I will completely blot out the memory of Amalek from under heaven.
Choose some men and go out to fight Amalek. Tomorrow I will stand on the top of the hill with the staff of God in my hand.

events.note: This is the first appearance of Joshua in the Bible. The Amalekites were descendants of Esau, nomads who roamed the Negev in the south and the Sinai wilderness. Deuteronomy says they attacked from behind those who were weary and lagging.
events.reflect: In the battle before me, which do I trust more, the hand that grips the sword or the hand raised to heaven, and when that hand sinks, do I know how to let the person beside me hold up my tired arms?

quiz.q: When Moses' arms grew tired, which two men held up his hands, one on each side?
quiz.explain: Aaron and Hur brought a stone for Moses to sit on and held up his hands, one on one side and one on the other (Ex 17:12).

img.title: Moses on the Mountain During the Battle
img.credit: James Tissot, Moses on the Mountain During the Battle, c. 1896–1902 · The Jewish Museum, New York · Public domain

events.title: Jethro's Advice
events.subtitle: An old priest's wisdom: do not carry it alone
story: Jethro, the priest of Midian, heard news of his son-in-law Moses. He brought Moses' wife Zipporah and his two sons, Gershom and Eliezer, to the camp at the foot of the mountain of God. Moses went out, bowed down to his father-in-law and kissed him, and told him everything the Lord had done.

Jethro rejoiced and declared that now he knew the Lord was greater than all gods. He offered a burnt offering and sacrifices to God, and Aaron came with all the elders of Israel to eat bread with him in the presence of God.

The next day Jethro watched Moses hear the people's disputes alone from morning till evening. This way you and the people will both wear out, he said; appoint trustworthy men and let them handle the small matters. Moses did as he said, and Jethro went back to his own country.

words.text: What you are doing is not good. You and the people with you will only wear yourselves out. The work is too heavy for you to carry alone.
Look among the people for capable men who fear God, who are honest and hate bribes, and appoint them as leaders over thousands, hundreds, fifties and tens.
Now I know that the Lord is greater than all other gods.

events.note: The text says Jethro came to where Moses was camped at the mountain of God. So views differ on whether this happened at Rephidim or after they reached Sinai. The Midianites are thought to have lived in northwestern Arabia, east of the Gulf of Aqaba.
events.reflect: What Jethro corrected was not Moses' laziness but his excessive zeal; could my diligence be taking away the places where others ought to stand?

quiz.q: Which of these was not among the leaders Jethro advised Moses to appoint?
quiz.explain: Jethro advised appointing leaders of thousands, hundreds, fifties and tens to judge the people (Ex 18:21). There were no leaders of five thousands.

img.title: Jethro and Moses
img.credit: James Tissot, Jethro and Moses, c. 1896–1902 · The Jewish Museum, New York · Public domain

events.title: God Comes Down on the Mountain
events.subtitle: A people carried on eagles' wings
story: In the third month after leaving Egypt, the people entered the Wilderness of Sinai and camped before the mountain. It was a silent land where peaks of red granite pierced the sky. When Moses went up the mountain, the Lord called to him and gave him words to pass on to Israel.

If you obey and keep my covenant, you will be my treasured possession, a kingdom of priests and a holy nation. With one voice the people answered that they would do everything the Lord had said. They washed their clothes, made themselves clean and waited for the third day. A boundary was set around the mountain.

On the morning of the third day there was thunder and lightning, a thick cloud covered the mountain, and a trumpet blast sounded loudly. Everyone in the camp trembled. The Lord came down in fire, and the mountain poured out smoke like a furnace and shook violently, while the trumpet grew louder and louder.

words.text: You have seen what I did to the Egyptians, and how I carried you to myself as an eagle carries its young on its wings.
The whole earth is mine, but if you truly listen to me and keep my covenant, you will be for me a kingdom of priests and a holy nation.
We will do everything the Lord has said.

events.note: Mount Sinai is traditionally identified with Jebel Musa, the Mountain of Moses, in the southern Sinai Peninsula, about 2,285 metres high. But other suggestions include Jebel Serbal, the northern part of the peninsula and mountains in northwestern Arabia, so the exact location is unknown.
events.reflect: Before giving the law, God first said he had carried them on eagles' wings and brought them to himself; do I know my life with God as a list of things to do, or as the story of a love that carried me here?

quiz.q: At Sinai, what did God say Israel would become if they kept the covenant?
options: A kingdom of priests and a holy nation
quiz.explain: If they kept the covenant, Israel would be God's treasured possession, a kingdom of priests and a holy nation (Ex 19:5–6).

img.title: Moses on Mount Sinai
img.credit: Jean-Léon Gérôme, Moses on Mount Sinai, c. 1895–1900 · Private collection · Public domain

events.title: The Ten Words
events.subtitle: Words from the one who set them free
story: From the mountain wrapped in smoke and fire, God himself spoke. His first words were not a command but an introduction. I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of Egypt, out of the house of slavery. On top of that rescue, ten words were laid down one by one.

Have no other gods but me. Do not make idols and bow down to them. Do not misuse my name. Remember the Sabbath and keep it holy. Honour your parents. Do not murder, do not commit adultery, do not steal, do not give false testimony, do not covet what belongs to your neighbour.

Seeing the thunder and lightning, hearing the trumpet and watching the smoking mountain, the people trembled and stood far off. They asked Moses to speak to them instead, for if God spoke to them directly they felt they would die. The people stayed at a distance, while Moses approached the thick darkness where God was.

words.text: I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of Egypt, out of the house of slavery. You shall have no other gods before me.
Honour your father and your mother, so that you may live long in the land the Lord your God is giving you.
You speak to us, and we will listen. If God speaks to us directly, we feel we will die.
Do not be afraid. God has come to test you, so that the fear of him will keep you from sinning.

events.note: Exodus 34 and Deuteronomy 4 call these the ten words. The way they are divided into ten differs slightly between the Jewish, Catholic and Lutheran, and Reformed traditions. The same words appear again in Deuteronomy 5.
events.reflect: If the ten words begin with the Lord who brought you out of the house of slavery, are the commandments a chain that binds me again, or a fence of freedom that keeps me from going back into slavery?

quiz.q: Which of the ten words comes with the promise that you may live long in the land?
quiz.explain: Honouring your parents came with the promise of a long life in the land the Lord was giving (Ex 20:12).

img.title: Moses and the Ten Commandments
img.credit: James Tissot, Moses and the Ten Commandments, c. 1896–1902 · The Jewish Museum, New York · Public domain

events.title: The Blood of the Covenant
events.subtitle: A covenant sealed in blood and shared at a meal
story: Moses told the people all the Lord's words, and with one voice they answered that they would do them. Early the next morning Moses built an altar at the foot of the mountain and set up twelve stone pillars for the twelve tribes of Israel. Young men offered burnt offerings and sacrificed bulls as fellowship offerings.

Moses put half of the blood in bowls and splashed the other half on the altar. When he read the book of the covenant aloud, the people said again: we will do everything the Lord has said, and we will obey. Moses sprinkled the blood from the bowls on the people and declared that this was the blood of the covenant.

Moses and Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, and seventy elders went up the mountain and saw the God of Israel. Under his feet was something like a pavement of sapphire, clear as the sky itself. They saw God, and they ate and drank. Then Moses entered the cloud and stayed on the mountain forty days and forty nights.

words.text: Come up to me on the mountain and wait there. I will give you the tablets of stone, with the law and commands I have written to teach the people.
Look, this is the blood of the covenant the Lord has made with you in keeping with all these words.
We will do everything the Lord has said, and we will obey.

events.note: In the ancient Near East, covenants were often made with a ceremony of slaughtering animals and eating together. The blood sprinkled at the making of the Sinai covenant points ahead to the blood of the covenant that Jesus spoke of when he lifted the cup at the Last Supper.
events.reflect: If the blood of the covenant was sprinkled over the people's vow to do everything, on the day my resolve collapses, do I lean on my own promise, or on his promise sealed in blood?

quiz.q: How many stone pillars did Moses set up beside the altar, one for each tribe of Israel?
quiz.explain: Moses built an altar at the foot of the mountain and set up twelve stone pillars for the twelve tribes of Israel (Ex 24:4).

img.title: Moses Forbids the People to Follow Him
img.credit: James Tissot, Moses Forbids the People to Follow Him, c. 1896–1902 · The Jewish Museum, New York · Public domain

events.title: The Golden Calf
events.subtitle: A god shaped by hands that could not bear to wait
story: When Moses did not come down from the mountain, the people crowded around Aaron. We do not know what has become of this Moses who brought us out, they said, so make us gods to go before us. Aaron collected their gold earrings, melted them down and shaped the image of a calf with a carving tool.

Israel, these are your gods who brought you out of Egypt. The next day the people offered burnt offerings, ate and drank, and got up to revel. On the mountain the Lord burned with anger, and Moses fell down and begged him to remember his promise to Abraham, Isaac and Israel. And the Lord relented.

Coming down with the two tablets that God himself had carved, Moses saw the singing and the dancing crowd. In his anger he smashed the tablets at the foot of the mountain, burned the calf, ground it to powder, scattered it on the water and made the people drink it. Then he went back up to the Lord and pleaded with him to forgive the people's sin.

words.text: Go down at once. Your people, whom you brought out of Egypt, have become corrupt. They have turned so quickly from the way I commanded, casting a calf and bowing down to it.
These people have committed a great sin. Now please forgive their sin. But if not, then blot my name out of the book you have written.
They gave me the gold, and I threw it into the fire, and out came this calf.

events.note: The golden calf is thought to be connected with Apis, the bull god of Egypt, or with the bull statues of Canaan seen as pedestals on which a god stood, and views differ. Later the same words are repeated before the golden calves Jeroboam set up at Bethel and Dan.
events.reflect: Like Aaron's excuse, “I threw the gold into the fire and out came this calf,” am I passing off an idol I shaped with my own hands as something that simply happened?

quiz.q: What did Moses do with the golden calf the people made?
options: Burned it, ground it to powder, scattered it on water and made them drink it
Threw it into the Red Sea
quiz.explain: Moses burned the calf in the fire, ground it to powder, scattered it on the water and made the Israelites drink it (Ex 32:20).

img.title: The Golden Calf
img.credit: James Tissot, The Golden Calf, c. 1896–1902 · The Jewish Museum, New York · Public domain

events.title: The Glory Passes By
events.subtitle: The name heard from a cleft in the rock
story: In a camp where the wound of the golden calf had not yet healed, Moses pleaded with the Lord again. If you will not go with us, do not send us up from here. Then he asked for something deeper still. Show me your glory.

No one may see my face and live. Instead, the Lord said he would put Moses in a cleft of the rock, cover him with his hand and pass by in front of him. Moses cut two stone tablets like the first ones and, in the dim light before dawn, climbed Mount Sinai alone.

The Lord came down in the cloud and stood there with him, and passed in front of him, proclaiming his name. A God compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, overflowing with love and faithfulness. Moses quickly bowed to the ground, and the Lord said he would renew his covenant.

words.text: The Lord, I am the Lord, a God compassionate and gracious, slow to anger and overflowing with steadfast love and faithfulness. I show love to a thousand generations and forgive wrongdoing and sin.
My presence will go with you, and I will give you rest.
Show me your glory.

events.note: This confession in Exodus 34:6–7 is the self-description of God most often echoed in the Old Testament. It is repeated in almost the same words in many places, including Numbers 14, Psalm 103 and Jonah 4.
events.reflect: When Moses asked to see his glory, God let him hear his name of compassion; while I ask God for wonders, do I actually want to know who he is?

quiz.q: Where did God put Moses as his glory passed by?
options: At the entrance of the tent of meeting
In a cleft of the rock
At the altar below the mountain
quiz.explain: The Lord said that as his glory passed by, he would put Moses in a cleft of the rock and cover him with his hand (Ex 33:22).

img.title: Moses with the Tablets of the Law
img.credit: Rembrandt, Moses with the Tablets of the Law, 1659 · Gemäldegalerie, Berlin · Public domain

events.title: Glory Fills the Tabernacle
events.subtitle: God's house set up in the middle of the wilderness
story: On the first day of the first month of the second year after leaving Egypt, the camp below Mount Sinai was busy from early morning. Silver bases were laid on the sand and gold-covered frames were raised one by one. When the curtains were hung and the goat-hair covering was spread, the house of God appeared in the heart of a tent village swaying in the wind.

Moses placed the tablets of the covenant in the ark and set the atonement cover on top. He put the table for the bread, the lampstand and the gold altar of incense in their places, and in the courtyard the altar of burnt offering and the basin. Down to setting up the curtains around the courtyard and hanging the screen at its gate, he finished everything just as the Lord had commanded.

Then the cloud covered the tent of meeting, and the glory of the Lord filled the tabernacle. Not even Moses could enter. From that day, whenever the cloud lifted from the tabernacle the people set out, and whenever the cloud stayed they stayed where they were. By day the cloud and by night the fire were before the eyes of all Israel.

words.text: On the first day of the first month, set up the tabernacle, the tent of meeting.
Dress Aaron in the sacred garments, anoint him and set him apart, so that he may serve me as priest.

events.note: The tabernacle was set up on the first day of the first month of the second year after the exodus, almost a year after leaving Egypt. Its courtyard was a hundred cubits long and fifty cubits wide, roughly 45 by 22 metres.
events.reflect: If the tent so full of glory that even Moses could not enter later came to us as the Word who pitched his tent among us, how lightly am I treating that presence?

quiz.q: When the cloud covered the tent of meeting and the glory of the Lord filled the tabernacle, what happened to Moses?
options: He could not enter the tent of meeting
quiz.explain: Because the cloud settled on the tent of meeting and the glory of the Lord filled the tabernacle, Moses could not enter the tent of meeting (Ex 40:35).

img.credit: James Tissot, Bezalel, c. 1896–1902 · The Jewish Museum, New York · Public domain

events.title: Graves of Craving
events.subtitle: Mouths that demanded meat became graves
story: Not long after they left Mount Sinai and entered the wilderness, complaining broke out at the edge of the camp. When the fire of the Lord blazed up, the people cried out, and when Moses prayed, the fire died down. They called the place Taberah. But among the mixed crowd that lived with them, craving began to spread again.

The fish they had eaten for free in Egypt, the cucumbers and melons, the leeks, onions and garlic. Staring at nothing but manna, which looked like coriander seed, the people wept at the door of every tent. Moses prayed as if he were collapsing. This burden is too heavy for me to carry alone. The Lord had him gather seventy elders, and he shared with them the Spirit that was on Moses.

A wind blew in from the sea, and flocks of quail piled up around the camp, a day's walk in every direction, two cubits deep on the ground. The people gathered them all that day, all night and all the next day without stopping. But while the meat was still between their teeth, the anger of the Lord broke out and a great plague struck. The place where those who had craved were buried was called Kibroth Hattaavah.

words.text: Is my arm too short? Now you will see with your own eyes whether my word comes true or not.
I will come down and speak with you there. I will take some of the Spirit that is on you and give it to them, so that you will not carry the burden of the people alone.
Are you jealous for my sake? I wish all the Lord's people were prophets and that the Lord would put his Spirit on them all.

events.note: Kibroth Hattaavah means graves of craving. Its exact location is unknown, but it is thought to lie somewhere northeast of Mount Sinai. Quail are migratory birds that cross the Sinai Peninsula in spring and autumn, and flocks exhausted from crossing the sea often come down low near the ground.
events.reflect: Before craving was a longing for what they lacked, it was weariness with what they had been given; am I tired of the grace I receive each day, longing for the tables of Egypt?

quiz.q: Which of these was not among the Egyptian foods the people longed for?
quiz.explain: The people longed for the fish, cucumbers, melons, leeks, onions and garlic they had eaten in Egypt (Num 11:5).

img.title: Moses Showing the Quails to the Israelites
img.credit: Andrea Schiavone, Moses Showing the Quails to the Israelites, c. 1545 · The Metropolitan Museum of Art · Public domain

events.title: The Twelve Spies
events.subtitle: They saw the same land and came back with different hearts
story: In the Wilderness of Paran, Moses sent twelve men into Canaan, one leader from each tribe. To Hoshea son of Nun he gave the name Joshua. In the season when the first grapes were ripening, they went up through the Negev in the south as far as Hebron, exploring the land for forty days.

The cluster of grapes they cut in the Valley of Eshcol was so large that two men carried it on a pole. They brought pomegranates and figs as well. It truly was a land flowing with milk and honey. But ten of the men said the cities were high and the descendants of Anak were like giants, and they had seemed like grasshoppers. Only Caleb cried out that they should go up at once.

That night the whole community wept aloud. There was even talk of choosing a leader to take them back to Egypt. Joshua and Caleb tore their clothes and said not to be afraid, for the Lord was with them, but the people wanted to stone them. Then the glory of the Lord appeared above the tent of meeting, and that generation was to walk in the wilderness for forty years.

words.text: My servant Caleb has a different spirit and has followed me wholeheartedly. I will bring him into the land he walked on, and his descendants will inherit it.
For the forty days you explored the land, a year for each day, you will bear the burden of your sins for forty years.
Let us go up right now and take the land. We can certainly overcome it.

events.note: Many identify Kadesh Barnea with the spring of Ain el Qudeirat south of the Negev, but there are other candidates nearby, such as Ain Qadeis, and views differ. Eshcol means cluster, and the valley is thought to be near Hebron.
events.reflect: What the ten men measured wrongly was not the giants' height but the size of God; while I measure my problems so precisely, how small am I measuring God?

quiz.q: What was the original name of the man Moses renamed Joshua?
quiz.explain: Moses gave Hoshea son of Nun the name Joshua (Num 13:16).

img.title: The Grapes of Canaan
img.credit: James Tissot, The Grapes of Canaan, c. 1896–1902 · The Jewish Museum, New York · Public domain

events.title: The Staff That Budded
events.subtitle: Almond blossoms on a dry stick
story: Korah of the tribe of Levi, with Dathan and Abiram of the tribe of Reuben, led two hundred and fifty well-known leaders to confront Moses and Aaron. The whole community is holy, they said, so why do you set yourselves above us? Dathan and Abiram even called Egypt a land flowing with milk and honey and refused to come when Moses summoned them.

As soon as Moses finished speaking, the ground under them split open, swallowed their tents and their people, and closed again. The two hundred and fifty men holding censers were consumed by fire from the Lord. The next day the people grumbled again and a plague spread, but when Aaron ran with his censer and stood between the dead and the living, the plague stopped.

The Lord had them place twelve staffs, one for each tribe, before the ark of the covenant. Aaron's name was written on the staff of Levi. The next morning, when Moses went into the tent of meeting, Aaron's staff had sprouted, blossomed and produced ripe almonds. Dead wood had come to life overnight.

words.text: The staff of the man I choose will sprout. In this way I will put an end to the grumbling of the Israelites against you.
Put Aaron's staff back in front of the ark of the covenant, as a sign to the rebellious.
This is how you will know that the Lord has sent me to do all these things, and that it was not my own idea.

events.note: In the land of Israel the almond tree is the first to blossom in late winter, which earned it a Hebrew name meaning the wakeful tree. The letter to the Hebrews says Aaron's budded staff was kept inside the ark of the covenant. The text does not say in which year of the wilderness journey this happened.
events.reflect: God did not argue with the rebels but made a dry staff blossom; where I long to be recognised, am I straining to prove myself, or waiting for the time he makes it bloom?

quiz.q: What fruit appeared on Aaron's staff overnight?
quiz.explain: Aaron's staff had sprouted, blossomed and produced almonds (Num 17:8).

img.title: The Punishment of Korah
img.credit: Sandro Botticelli, The Punishment of Korah, 1481–1482 · Sistine Chapel · Public domain

events.title: The Waters of Meribah
events.subtitle: A hand that struck the rock twice
story: In the first month the Israelites arrived in the Wilderness of Zin and stayed at Kadesh. There Miriam died and was buried. She was the sister of Moses and Aaron, the prophet who had taken up her tambourine and sung before the women on the day they crossed the sea. Before the grief had passed, the camp ran out of water.

The people crowded around Moses and Aaron and quarrelled with them. Why did you drag us to this terrible place? There is no grain, no figs, no grapes, no pomegranates, not even water to drink. When the two of them fell face down at the entrance to the tent of meeting, the glory of the Lord appeared, and the Lord told Moses to take his staff and speak to the rock in front of the community.

But Moses shouted at the people gathered before the rock, Listen, you rebels. Then he raised his hand and struck the rock twice with his staff. Water gushed out, and the community and their animals drank. But that day Moses and Aaron heard that they would not enter the promised land. People called that water Meribah.

words.text: Take the staff and gather the community. Speak to that rock as they watch, and it will pour out its water.
You did not trust me enough to show my holiness before the people. So you will not bring this community into the land I have given them.
Listen, you rebels. Must we bring water out of this rock for you?

events.note: Meribah means quarrelling. The text says only the first month, but since Aaron died in the fifth month of the fortieth year in the wilderness, this event is thought to belong to that year too. Early in the exodus, at Rephidim, water had also come from a rock, and that place too was called Meribah.
events.reflect: The same rock, the same staff, yet this time God said to speak to the rock; by clinging to what worked last time, am I missing the way God wants now?

quiz.q: What did the Lord tell Moses to do before the rock?
options: Strike the rock once with his staff
Build an altar before the rock
quiz.explain: The Lord told him to speak to the rock in front of the community, but Moses struck the rock twice with his staff (Num 20:8, 11).

img.title: Moses Smites the Rock in the Desert
img.credit: James Tissot, Moses Smites the Rock in the Desert, c. 1896–1902 · The Jewish Museum, New York · Public domain

events.title: Aaron on Mount Hor
events.subtitle: The high priest's robes pass to his son
story: The whole community of Israel left Kadesh and came to Mount Hor on the border of Edom. The red rock mountain glowed as if on fire in the evening sun. There the Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron. It was time for Aaron to be gathered to his ancestors, and because of what happened at the waters of Meribah he would not enter the land.

Moses took Aaron and his son Eleazar and climbed the mountain as the whole community watched. The shadows of the three men stretched long as they climbed the stony slope. On the summit Moses took the high priest's garments off his brother one by one and put them on Eleazar. They were the robes in which Aaron had stood before the altar for nearly forty years, bearing the sins of the people.

Aaron died there on the mountaintop. Only Moses and Eleazar came down. When all Israel learned that Aaron had died, they mourned for him thirty days. The wilderness wind swept through the camp, and young Eleazar, wearing the priest's robes, stood in the middle of their weeping.

words.text: Aaron will now be gathered to his ancestors. Because you rebelled against my word at the waters of Meribah, he will not enter the land I have given the Israelites.
Remove Aaron's garments and put them on his son Eleazar. Aaron will die there and be gathered to his ancestors.

events.note: Numbers 33 says Aaron died on the first day of the fifth month of the fortieth year after the exodus, at the age of one hundred and twenty-three. Tradition identifies Mount Hor with Jebel Harun near Petra, where a shrine to Aaron's tomb stands, but others place it at a mountain nearer Kadesh, so the location is uncertain.
events.reflect: Aaron never set foot in the promised land, yet his robes passed on to the next generation; can I rejoice more that God's work goes on than that my name remains?

quiz.q: Who put on Aaron's priestly garments on Mount Hor?
quiz.explain: Moses took off Aaron's garments and put them on his son Eleazar, and Aaron died on the mountaintop (Num 20:28).

img.title: The Death of Aaron
img.credit: James Tissot, The Death of Aaron, c. 1896–1902 · The Jewish Museum, New York · Public domain

events.title: The Bronze Snake on a Pole
events.subtitle: Look and live
story: Leaving Mount Hor, Israel turned toward the Red Sea road to go around the land of Edom. With the promised land right in front of them, they were heading south again. The hot wind of the Arabah blew the sand about, and on the road the people's patience gradually ran out.

They poured it all out against God and Moses. Why did you bring us out to die in the wilderness? There is no food and no water, and we are sick of this miserable food. Then venomous snakes came into the camp and bit the people, and many died. The people came to Moses, confessed their sin and begged him to pray for them.

When Moses prayed, the Lord spoke. Make the shape of a venomous snake and put it on a pole; anyone who is bitten and looks at it will live. Moses made a snake out of bronze and raised it high on the top of a pole. Whenever someone who had been bitten lifted his head and looked at the bronze snake, he lived.

words.text: Make the shape of a venomous snake and fix it on a pole. Anyone who has been bitten by a snake will live if they look at it.
We sinned when we spoke against the Lord and against you. Pray to the Lord to take these snakes away from us.

events.note: The text does not say where the bronze snake was set up, but following the list of stages in Numbers 33 it is placed at Punon in the Arabah. Punon is thought to be Feinan in present-day Jordan, the site of ancient copper mines. Centuries later King Hezekiah broke the bronze snake in pieces because people were burning incense to it.
events.reflect: What saved the people was not the power of the bronze snake but eyes lifted up to look, and Jesus said he too must be lifted up in the same way; am I staring only at my own wounds, or lifting my head to look at him?

quiz.q: How could a person bitten by a venomous snake live?
options: By receiving Moses' laying on of hands
By offering a lamb on the altar
By looking at the bronze snake on the pole
By going outside the camp to wash
quiz.explain: Whenever someone bitten by a snake looked at the bronze snake, they lived (Num 21:9).

img.title: The Brazen Serpent
img.credit: James Tissot, The Brazen Serpent, c. 1896–1902 · The Jewish Museum, New York · Public domain

events.title: Winning the Land East of the Jordan
events.subtitle: A battle that began on the King's Highway
story: Having made their way around the wilderness, Israel stood north of the Arnon Valley, before the land of Sihon king of the Amorites. Israel sent messengers with a polite request. We will not go into your fields or vineyards or drink water from your wells; just let us pass along the King's Highway. But Sihon would not let them through.

Sihon led out all his people into the wilderness and fought Israel at Jahaz. Israel struck him with the sword and took his land from the Arnon to the Jabbok River. Israel also settled in Heshbon, Sihon's royal city, and the villages around it. An old song had sung that fire went out from Heshbon and consumed Moab.

Then Israel went up north toward Bashan. Og king of Bashan came out to Edrei with his whole army. The Lord told Moses not to be afraid, and Israel struck down Og, his sons and all his people and took his land. For the first time, the high plains east of the Jordan became the land of Israel.

words.text: Do not be afraid of him. I have handed him over to you, with his people and his land. Do to him as you did to Sihon king of the Amorites, who ruled in Heshbon.
Let us pass through your land. We will not go into any field or vineyard or drink water from any well. We will keep to the King's Highway.

events.note: Heshbon is identified with Tell Hesban, north of Madaba in Jordan, but excavations have found no clear remains of a town from this period, so views differ. The southern border, the Arnon, is today's Wadi Mujib, and the northern border, the Jabbok, is the Zarqa River.
events.reflect: When their request to pass along the King's Highway was refused, God turned that blocked road into their first inheritance; standing before a closed door, do I have eyes to see what has been prepared beyond it?

quiz.q: Og, whom Israel defeated at Edrei, was king of which land?
quiz.explain: Og king of Bashan came out to fight at Edrei, and Israel struck him down and took his land (Num 21:33, 35).

img.title: The Conquest of the Amorites
img.credit: James Tissot, The Conquest of the Amorites, c. 1896–1902 · The Jewish Museum, New York · Public domain

events.title: Balaam and the Donkey
events.subtitle: Blessing pours from a mouth that came to curse
story: When Israel camped on the plains of Moab, across the Jordan from Jericho, Balak king of Moab was gripped by fear. He sent for Balaam son of Beor, who lived at Pethor by the Euphrates. Envoys came carrying the fee for divination and asked him to curse this people.

After a second group of envoys came, Balaam saddled his donkey and set out. But the donkey suddenly turned off the road, crushed his foot against a wall, and finally lay down. The angel of the Lord was standing in the road with his sword drawn. After she had been beaten three times, the Lord opened the donkey's mouth, and she spoke to her master.

Balak took Balaam to high places, and on seven altars they offered bulls and rams. But every time Balaam opened his mouth, blessings poured out instead of curses. How beautiful are your tents, Jacob. At last he prophesied that a star would come out of Jacob. Balak clapped his hands in fury, but Balaam went back to his own home.

words.text: Do not go with them. You must not curse that people, for they are blessed.
Since these men have come to summon you, get up and go with them. But say only what I tell you.
I see him, but not now; I look at him, but not near. A star will come out of Jacob, and a scepter will rise out of Israel.

events.note: A plaster inscription found in 1967 at Deir Alla in the Jordan Valley mentions a seer named Balaam son of Beor. Written around the eighth century BC, it shows that Balaam was long remembered east of the Jordan. Pethor is thought to have been near the upper Euphrates.
events.reflect: The donkey saw the angel blocking the road while the famous seer did not; so absorbed in my own plans, am I treating the stop signs God puts up as nothing but annoying interruptions?

quiz.q: Why did Balaam's donkey turn off the road and finally lie down?
options: The angel of the Lord with a sword was blocking the road
There was a snake on the road
quiz.explain: The donkey saw the angel of the Lord standing in the road with a drawn sword, and turned off the road (Num 22:23).

img.credit: James Tissot, Balaam and the Ass, c. 1896–1902 · The Jewish Museum, New York · Public domain

events.title: Hear, O Israel
events.subtitle: Words to engrave on the heart and write on the doorposts
story: The eleventh month of the fortieth year, in the land of Moab east of the Jordan. Across the river the palm groves of Jericho could be seen in the distance. The new generation, born and raised in the wilderness, gathered before the aged Moses. With the last of his strength, Moses spoke to them the words they must keep in the land they were about to enter.

Hear, O Israel. The Lord our God is one. Love him with all your heart, all your soul and all your strength. Engrave these words on your heart, and tell them to your children when you sit at home and when you walk along the road, when you lie down and when you get up. Tie them on your wrists, bind them on your foreheads, and write them on the doorposts of your houses and on your gates.

Moses did not forget to warn them. When you have great cities you did not build, houses full of good things you did not fill, wells you did not dig and vineyards you did not plant, and you eat your fill, do not forget the Lord who brought you out of slavery. And when your children ask one day what these words mean, start by telling them that we were Pharaoh's slaves in Egypt.

words.text: Hear, O Israel. The Lord our God, the Lord is one. Love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul and with all your strength.
Keep these words I give you today in your heart. Repeat them to your children, and talk about them when you are at home and when you are on the road, when you lie down and when you get up.
Then be careful. Do not forget the Lord who brought you out of Egypt, the land of slavery.

events.note: The Hebrew word Shema, meaning hear, became the name of this confession. Jews still recite these words morning and evening and fix small cases containing scripture to their doorposts. Jesus named Deuteronomy 6:5 the greatest commandment, and he quoted this chapter during his testing in the wilderness.
events.reflect: The words that begin with “Hear” pass through “Love” and go on to “Do not forget”; on full and comfortable days, does my faith still remember why I love God?

quiz.q: When children ask the meaning of these laws, what were the parents to tell them first?
options: We received the law at Sinai
We were Pharaoh's slaves in Egypt
We walked forty years in the wilderness
quiz.explain: When your children ask, answer that we were Pharaoh's slaves in Egypt, but the Lord brought us out with a mighty hand (Deut 6:20–21).

img.title: Moses and Joshua in the Tabernacle
img.credit: James Tissot, Moses and Joshua in the Tabernacle, c. 1896–1902 · The Jewish Museum, New York · Public domain

events.title: The Land Seen from Mount Nebo
events.subtitle: A river he did not cross, a land he gazed on to the end
story: Leaving the plains of Moab behind, Moses climbed Mount Nebo alone. On the summit of Pisgah, facing Jericho, the wind swept over the dry grass. He was a hundred and twenty years old, yet his eyes were not dim and his strength had not failed.

The Lord showed him the whole land. From Gilead in the north to Dan, the hill country of Naphtali, Ephraim and Manasseh, the land of Judah reaching to the western sea, the Negev in the south, and the valley of Jericho, the city of palms, as far as Zoar. Beyond the shimmering haze, the promise lay spread out.

There in the land of Moab, Moses died as the Lord had said, and the Lord buried him in the valley opposite Beth Peor. To this day no one knows where his grave is. The people wept for thirty days, and Joshua, on whom Moses had laid his hands, followed him, filled with the spirit of wisdom.

words.text: This is the land I swore to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob that I would give to their descendants. I have let you see it with your own eyes, but you will not cross over into it.
Since then no prophet like Moses has risen in Israel, whom the Lord knew face to face.

events.note: Mount Nebo is thought to be a peak in Jordan a little over 700 metres high. On a clear day the Dead Sea, the oasis of Jericho and even the ridges toward Jerusalem can be seen from it. Pisgah is taken to be the name for the summit of that range.
events.reflect: If Moses, who could only look at the land from Mount Nebo, later stood in it with Jesus on the mountain of the transfiguration, can I entrust the promises I will not see fulfilled in my lifetime to God's longer time?

quiz.q: How old was Moses when he died?
quiz.explain: Moses was a hundred and twenty years old when he died, yet his eyes were not dim and his strength had not left him (Deut 34:7). A hundred and ten was Joshua's age when he died.

img.title: Moses Sees the Promised Land from Afar
img.credit: James Tissot, Moses Sees the Promised Land from Afar, c. 1896–1902 · The Jewish Museum, New York · Public domain

events.title: Be Strong and Courageous
events.subtitle: A voice heard again where Moses had been
story: The camp east of the Jordan, after Moses' funeral. The tents lay quiet in the shade of the acacia trees. Then the Lord spoke to Joshua son of Nun, who had served Moses. My servant Moses is dead. Now get up and cross the Jordan with all this people.

From the wilderness and Lebanon to the great river Euphrates, and to the great sea in the west, will be your land. The Lord promised to be with Joshua as he had been with Moses, and told him again and again to keep the book of the law always on his lips and to meditate on it day and night.

Joshua ordered the officers to prepare provisions, for within three days they would cross the Jordan. The fighting men of Reuben, Gad and the half tribe of Manasseh, who had received land east of the Jordan, answered that they would cross ahead of their brothers. Only be strong and courageous, their voices rang through the camp.

words.text: Have I not commanded you? Be strong and courageous. Do not be afraid or discouraged, for I, the Lord your God, am with you wherever you go.
As I was with Moses, so I will be with you. I will not leave you, and I will never abandon you.
Keep the words of this book of the law always on your lips and turn them over day and night. Then your way will open before you, and you will act wisely.
Whatever you command us we will do, and wherever you send us we will go. Only be strong and courageous.

events.note: The name Joshua means the Lord is salvation. Moses gave it to him in place of his original name, Hoshea. In Greek it becomes the same name as Jesus. Shittim means acacias, and its exact location remains a matter of conjecture.
events.reflect: God said “Be strong and courageous” again and again, likely because Joshua was that afraid; do I think I can obey only once my fear is gone, or do I hold on to the word and go forward while still afraid?

quiz.q: Within how many days did Joshua tell the people they would cross the Jordan?
quiz.explain: Joshua commanded, Get your provisions ready, for within three days you will cross this Jordan (Josh 1:11).
