img.credit: James Tissot, Moses Blesses Joshua Before the High Priest, c. 1896–1902 · The Jewish Museum, New York · Public domain

events.title: Rahab's Scarlet Cord
events.subtitle: A single thread of faith hanging from a window in the wall
story: Two spies sent from Shittim slipped into Jericho, the city of palms. They stayed at Rahab's house, built into the city wall. Word travelled fast. At sunset the king's men knocked at her door and demanded that she hand the men over.

Rahab hid the two men under stalks of flax she had laid out to dry on the roof, and told the king's men they had left about the time the gate was shut. After the pursuers had run off toward the fords of the Jordan, she went up to the roof and confessed. We heard how the Lord dried up the Red Sea, and our hearts melted.

Rahab let them down by a rope through the window to the outside of the wall. The spies made a promise. When we come into this land, tie this scarlet cord in the window and gather your family inside the house. After hiding in the hills for three days, they returned and said, The Lord has given the whole land into our hands.

words.text: The Lord your God is God in heaven above and on the earth below.
I have shown you kindness, so swear to me by the Lord. Show kindness to my father's household too, and save our lives from death.
Our lives for yours. When the Lord gives us this land, we will deal faithfully with you.

events.note: Jericho is an oasis city in the Jordan Valley about 250 metres below sea level, counted among the oldest towns in the world. The flax drying on the roof recalls the spring harvest season. Rahab's name also appears in the genealogy of Jesus in Matthew's Gospel.
events.reflect: If a woman who lived in the city wall found her name in the Messiah's family line through a single scarlet cord, am I filtering out in advance, by my own standards, the people God may use?

quiz.q: What did Rahab tie in her window as a sign that she would be saved?
quiz.explain: The spies told Rahab to tie a scarlet cord in the window through which she had let them down (Josh 2:18, 21).

img.title: The Harlot of Jericho and the Two Spies
img.credit: James Tissot, The Harlot of Jericho and the Two Spies, c. 1896–1902 · The Jewish Museum, New York · Public domain

events.title: Crossing the Jordan
events.subtitle: The waters stop, and stones become memory
story: At the spring harvest the Jordan was swollen enough to overflow its banks. The people waited three days beside the river as its muddy water rushed past. Joshua said, Consecrate yourselves, for tomorrow the Lord will do wonders among you.

The moment the feet of the priests carrying the ark of the covenant touched the water's edge, the water flowing from upstream piled up like a dam far away near the town of Adam and stopped. While the priests stood on dry ground in the middle of the river, all the people crossed over opposite Jericho. The only sound was feet on pebbles.

Twelve men, chosen from each tribe, each carried a stone up from the riverbed and set them up at Gilgal. There the people were circumcised and kept the Passover on the evening of the fourteenth day of the first month. The day after they ate the produce of the land, the manna that had fallen for forty years stopped.

words.text: Today I will begin to raise you up in the sight of all Israel, so that they will know that I am with you as I was with Moses.
Today I have rolled away from you the disgrace of Egypt.
When your children ask one day what these stones mean, tell them: Israel crossed this Jordan on dry ground.

events.note: The Jordan rises highest in spring, when the snows of Mount Hermon melt. The town of Adam is thought to be Tell ed Damiyeh, about 30 kilometres upstream, and there are records that during an earthquake in 1927 the banks nearby collapsed and blocked the river for a time. Views on the location of Gilgal differ.
events.reflect: The river stopped only after the priests' feet touched the water; do I wait to move until I see the whole way open, or do I take the first step into water that is still flowing?

quiz.q: After keeping the Passover at Gilgal and eating the produce of the land, what stopped the next day?
quiz.explain: The manna stopped the day after they ate the produce of the land, and from that year Israel ate the crops of Canaan (Josh 5:12).

img.title: Joshua Passing the River Jordan with the Ark of the Covenant
img.credit: Benjamin West, Joshua Passing the River Jordan with the Ark of the Covenant, 1800 · Art Gallery of New South Wales · Public domain

events.title: The Walls Fall
events.subtitle: Seven days of silence before the shout
story: Jericho was tightly shut. No one went in or out, and the morning sun shone on its walls. The Lord said to Joshua, See, I have handed Jericho over to you, with its king and its warriors. But the way would be not the sword, but walking.

Once a day for six days, seven priests carrying rams' horn trumpets marched around the city ahead of the ark, blowing the trumpets. The people did not say a word. At dawn on the seventh day they circled the city seven times, and at the long blast of the trumpets all the people shouted. The walls collapsed.

The text records, briefly and heavily, that every life and all the goods in the city were devoted to the Lord and destroyed. In the midst of it all, only the house with the scarlet cord was left standing. Rahab and her family were rescued as promised, and from that day on they lived among Israel.

words.text: See, I have handed Jericho over to you, with its king and its warriors.
When the priests sound a long blast on the rams' horns and you hear it, have all the people give a great shout. Then the wall will collapse.
Shout! The Lord has given you the city.

events.note: Archaeologists disagree about Jericho's fallen walls. In the 1930s Garstang argued for a destruction around 1400 BC, Kenyon held that there was no walled city at that time, and later some scholars again supported the earlier date.
events.reflect: For six days, when nothing seemed to happen, they kept marching in silence; how long can I quietly keep up an obedience whose fruit I cannot yet see?

quiz.q: How many times did Israel march around Jericho on the seventh day?
quiz.explain: For six days they went around the city once a day, and on the seventh day they went around it seven times (Josh 6:3–4, 15).

img.title: The Seven Trumpets of Jericho
img.credit: James Tissot, The Seven Trumpets of Jericho, c. 1896–1902 · The Jewish Museum, New York · Public domain

events.title: Achan's Sin and the City of Ai
events.subtitle: When one hidden thing brings down a whole camp
story: After the victory at Jericho, three thousand men went up to Ai, a small town east of Bethel. But they were driven back from the city gate and fled down the slope, and thirty-six of them fell. The people's hearts melted like water. Joshua tore his clothes and lay face down before the ark until evening.

The Lord said, Get up. Israel has sinned. The lot narrowed from tribe to clan, from clan to family, and finally fell on Achan of the tribe of Judah. He confessed that he had coveted a fine robe from Shinar, silver and a bar of gold, and had buried them in the ground inside his tent.

Achan and all that belonged to him came to an end under stones in the Valley of Achor, and a great heap of stones was raised over them. After that the Lord told Joshua not to be afraid. Soldiers lying in ambush behind the city captured Ai, and the text says the city was burned and remains a heap of ruins to this day.

words.text: Get up. Why are you lying on your face like this? Israel has sinned. They have broken the covenant I commanded, stolen what was devoted to me and hidden it among their own belongings.
Do not be afraid or discouraged. Take the whole army and go up to Ai. I have handed over to you the king of Ai, his people, his city and his land.
It is true. I have sinned against the Lord, the God of Israel. I saw those things, I wanted them and I took them. They are buried in the ground inside my tent.

events.note: Ai means heap of ruins. It has traditionally been identified with et Tell, but that site turned out to be uninhabited in the Late Bronze Age, so some suggest other candidates such as Khirbet el Maqatir. The location is still debated.
events.reflect: What Achan hid was a cloak, some silver and a bar of gold, yet the whole camp was shaken; can I admit that a hidden sin I thought was only my own business is weighing on my community?

quiz.q: Where did Achan hide the things he had stolen?
options: In the ground inside his tent
quiz.explain: Achan confessed that the robe, the silver and the gold bar were hidden in the ground inside his tent (Josh 7:21–22).

img.title: Ai Is Taken by Joshua
img.credit: James Tissot, Ai Is Taken by Joshua, c. 1896–1902 · The Jewish Museum, New York · Public domain

events.title: Covenant Between Two Mountains
events.subtitle: Words heard by two mountains facing each other
story: The valley of Shechem cuts deep between two mountains, Mount Ebal to the north and Mount Gerizim to the south. As Moses had commanded, Joshua built an altar on Mount Ebal of uncut stones that no iron tool had touched, and offered burnt offerings and fellowship offerings to the Lord.

There he copied the law of Moses onto the stones. The Levitical priests carrying the ark of the covenant stood in the middle, with half the people in front of Mount Gerizim and half in front of Mount Ebal. Elders, officials and judges were all there, and even the foreigners who lived among them.

Joshua read every word of the law. The words of blessing and the words of curse crossed the valley and echoed off the slopes of the two mountains. Women and children, and even those who had come from other nations, heard every word that day.

words.text: If you build an altar of stones for me, do not build it with cut stones. If you use a tool on the stones, you defile it.
See, today I am setting before you a blessing and a curse. When you enter the land, proclaim the blessing on Mount Gerizim and the curse on Mount Ebal.
Of all that Moses had commanded, there was not a word that Joshua did not read before the whole assembly. The women, the children and the foreigners heard it too.

events.note: Shechem lies in the pass between Mount Ebal, about 940 metres high, and Mount Gerizim, a little over 880 metres. It is also where Abraham built his first altar in Canaan. Some regard a stone structure excavated on Mount Ebal in the 1980s as Joshua's altar, but the debate continues.
events.reflect: Blessing and curse echoed together between two mountains, and even women, children and foreigners heard every word; am I looking only toward the mountain that is easy to hear?

quiz.q: On which mountain did Joshua build the altar?
quiz.explain: Joshua built an altar to the Lord on Mount Ebal from stones no iron tool had touched (Josh 8:30–31).

events.title: Sun, Stand Still
events.subtitle: The day the Lord listened to one man's prayer
story: When he heard that Gibeon had made peace with Israel, Adoni Zedek king of Jerusalem called together the kings of Hebron, Jarmuth, Lachish and Eglon. The armies of the five kings surrounded Gibeon. The Gibeonites hurriedly sent word to Joshua at Gilgal. Come up quickly and save us.

Joshua marched up the mountain road all night and fell on them at dawn. The Lord threw the enemy into confusion, and as they fled down the slope of Beth Horon, great hailstones poured from the sky on them. The text notes that more died from the hail than from the sword.

That day Joshua spoke to the Lord in the sight of all Israel. Sun, stand still over Gibeon. Moon, stop over the Valley of Aijalon. The sun stopped in the middle of the sky and did not go down for about a whole day. There has never been a day like it, before or since, when the Lord listened to the voice of a man.

words.text: Do not be afraid of them. I have handed them over to you; not one of them will be able to stand against you.
Sun, stand still over Gibeon. Moon, stop over the Valley of Aijalon.
Do not abandon your servants. Come up quickly, save us and help us.

events.note: Gibeon is el Jib, about nine kilometres northwest of Jerusalem, where jar handles inscribed with the name Gibeon and a large water pool have been excavated. As for the sun standing still, views differ: some take it as a literal miracle, others as poetic language quoted from the Book of Jashar.
events.reflect: The covenant with Gibeon was made through deception, yet Joshua climbed the mountain road all night to keep it; am I someone who keeps a promise to the end even when it has turned against me?

quiz.q: Where did Joshua tell the moon to stop?
quiz.explain: Joshua cried out, Sun, stand still over Gibeon, and moon, over the Valley of Aijalon (Josh 10:12).

img.title: Joshua Commanding the Sun to Stand Still
img.credit: John Martin, Joshua Commanding the Sun to Stand Still, c. 1840 · Yale Center for British Art · Public domain

events.title: Dividing the Land at Shiloh
events.subtitle: Writing the promise onto the map
story: Shiloh, a quiet hill in the hill country of Ephraim. The whole community of Israel gathered there and set up the tent of meeting. The land lay subdued before them, but seven tribes still hesitated, without having received their share.

Joshua asked, How long will you put off going to take the land the Lord has given you? He chose three men from each tribe to travel through the land, divide it into seven parts and write a description. The Levites received no share, for the priestly service of the Lord was their inheritance.

The men walked over hills and through valleys, writing down the name of every town in a book. When they came back to the camp at Shiloh with their scroll, Joshua cast lots before the Lord and gave the remaining tribes their land. At last the promise became land with names.

words.text: How long will you put off going to take possession of the land the Lord, the God of your ancestors, has given you?
Divide the land into seven parts, write them down and bring the description to me. I will cast lots for you here before the Lord our God.
The Levites will receive no share among you, because the priestly service of the Lord is their inheritance.

events.note: Shiloh is identified with Khirbet Seilun, about 30 kilometres north of Jerusalem. The tent of meeting remained there throughout the time of the judges, and the story of Eli and Hannah in 1 Samuel is also set at Shiloh. The exact spot where the tabernacle stood is unknown.
events.reflect: If the land had already been given and seven tribes still put off going to take it, am I putting off enjoying the grace God has already given me, with the excuse of “not yet”?

quiz.q: Into how many parts did Joshua have the remaining land divided and written down?
quiz.explain: For the seven tribes that had not yet received their inheritance, he had the land divided into seven parts and written down (Josh 18:2, 6, 9).

events.title: As for Me and My House
events.subtitle: The last question of an old leader
story: Many years later, Joshua called all the tribes of Israel together at Shechem. The elders, leaders, judges and officials stood before God. He told them the story in order, from the house of Terah beyond the river, through Abraham, Egypt and the wilderness, down to that very day.

I gave you a land you did not labour for, towns you did not build, vineyards and olive groves you did not plant. Then Joshua asked them. Choose today whom you will serve. As for me and my house, we will serve the Lord. Again and again the people answered, We too will serve the Lord.

That day Joshua made a covenant and wrote it in the book of the law of God. He took a large stone and set it up under the oak beside the sanctuary. This stone will be our witness. Some time later he died at the age of a hundred and ten and was buried at Timnath Serah in the hill country of Ephraim.

words.text: I gave you a land you had not laboured for and towns you had not built. You live in them and eat the fruit of vineyards and olive groves you did not plant.
Choose for yourselves today whom you will serve. But as for me and my house, we will serve the Lord.
We will serve the Lord our God and listen to his voice.

events.note: Shechem is Tell Balata near present-day Nablus, where Jacob once buried foreign idols under an oak. Scholars note that this covenant ceremony, moving from a review of history to demands, witnesses and a written record, resembles the form of ancient Near Eastern treaties.
events.reflect: Before pressing the people to decide, Joshua first declared his own household's choice; before I demand it of others, am I first showing whom my house serves?

quiz.q: How old was Joshua when he died?
quiz.explain: Joshua son of Nun died at the age of a hundred and ten and was buried at Timnath Serah (Josh 24:29–30). A hundred and twenty was Moses' age when he died.
